title: Growth & development
objectives: Plot normal growth velocity and state when head circumference stops being the lead parameter.
List red-flag developmental milestones that alter surgical timing.
Explain catch-up growth after chronic disease and what blunts it.
body_md:
### Why this area matters

No recent paper asks growth charts directly — which is exactly why a short, confident paragraph scores when development affects a surgical decision (timing of orchidopexy, elective surgery in a malnourished child, adolescent bariatric selection).

### The exam-usable core

Growth velocity peaks in infancy, steadies through childhood, and surges at puberty; crossing centiles downward matters more than any single point. Chronic disease (IBD-type malabsorption, CKD, cyanotic heart disease, chronic sepsis) flattens velocity first and weight before height — catch-up follows cure only if nutrition, hormones and chronic inflammation all normalise. Head circumference tracks brain growth and matters most under two years; macro/microcephaly in a surgical neonate should trigger a neurodevelopmental look before elective timing is fixed.

Developmental milestones decide fitness and consent conversations, not operative steps: global delay changes anaesthetic planning, postoperative expectations and follow-up intensity. Adolescence adds capacity assessment for assent, bariatric candidacy and transition planning.

### How it is asked

Rarely standalone — usually one sub-part stapled to nutrition, chronic disease or adolescent surgery. Answer with one velocity statement, one centile-crossing rule, and one sentence tying it to the case in front of you.
